5 expert takeaways on 2026 midterm election security
Politics
Updated on Oct 30, 2026 6:09 PM EDT — Published on
Oct 29, 2026 5:35 PM EDT
Correction: This story has been updated to clarify details around Votebeat's investigation into claims of fraud in Pennsylvania's 2024 presidential results, including misattribution of a statistical model. We regret the error.
With Election Day around the corner, states have been working hard to prepare, with some adopting new congressional maps and voting rules on top of normal election security measures.
While President Donald Trump persists in making unfounded claims about the security and integrity of the nation's elections, the Department of Justice is planning to send 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states, more than double the number dispatched during the 2022 midterms.
READ MORE: How some states are responding to DOJ's plan to send 1,000 monitors on Election Day
As part of our coverage of the midterm groundwork happening across the country, PBS News' Liz Landers and Votebeat editorial director Jessica Huseman hosted a Reddit "Ask Me Anything" Q&A on Wednesday to address people's questions on election security.
Educate your inbox
Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics
newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else.
Several questions touched on people's concerns about their vote being tampered with or not being counted, alongside broader concerns about possible meddling from the federal government.
The Trump administration is attempting measures that haven't been tried before, Huseman said. Those actions include attempts to change election rules through executive orders, repeated demands for voter data and efforts to expand the government's role – specifically the executive branch – in elections. All of this amounts to an "unprecedented environment now," she said.
And yet, "elections officials are confident the system will hold," she added.
Here are five major takeaways from the Reddit AMA.
Evidence shows that illegal voting is extremely rare
Ballots for the upcoming midterm elections are stacked inside a locked, secured and monitored cage at the Durham County Board of Elections, as election officials boost security to fortify the building and protect staff in preparation for the upcoming midterm elections, in Durham, North Carolina, on Aug. 31, 2026. Photo by Jonathan Drake/ Reuters
Trump has routinely cast doubt on the security of the vote, making false claims of " rampant" voter fraud even a week ahead of Nov. 3.
The president, who has continued to falsely claim that the 2020 presidential election was "rigged," has fixated on rooting out what he claims is election fraud this election cycle. The Trump administration has issued more than 100 subpoenas to more than a dozen states requesting voter roll data, expanding its efforts to tamp down alleged noncitizen voting. But illegal voting by noncitizens voting is vanishingly rare.
READ MORE: Trump's focus on noncitizen voting has led to 160 arrests. That shows it's rare, experts say
Votebeat spent more than a year investigating claims from a nonprofit group called the Election Truth Alliance that promoted a researcher's statistical analysis suggesting votes in the 2024 election had been manipulated in Pennsylvania, she said.
Much of that analysis did not stand up to scrutiny, Votebeat's reporting found.
WATCH: Inside Georgia's push to rebuild trust in elections after Trump's false claims
Huseman said it's worth remembering that "elections are not black boxes."
"In the places where the Election Truth Alliance alleged truly incredible problems, there were audits, observers, paper ballots and an entire staff of people whose jobs are ensuring the accuracy of these numbers," she said. "We can scrutinize the evidence as it's presented, but when we have it, we have to look it squarely in the face and call it what it is."
Trump can't declare a national emergency to interfere with elections
Nowhere in the U.S. Constitution does the president of the United States have express authority over how elections are run.
As laid out in the country's founding document, states determine the time, place and manner of elections. And Congress has a role in passing legislation over federal elections, though they have not passed major laws like this in a while, Landers said.
READ MORE: Immigrants seeking U.S. citizenship targeted in Trump administration's illegal voting crackdown
To put a finer point on it: The president cannot declare some kind of national emergency and expect all 50 states to stop their elections.
"I know from speaking with election officials across the country that they will not stop their election administration just because the president declared something over a process he does not have any legal authority," Landers said.
She also asked Trump in February if he would declare a national emergency — as some of his allies have urged. He said no at the time, adding he'd never heard about that.
Federal election monitors are there to observe
The Justice Department is planning to dispatch more than 1,000 federal election monitors to observe proceedings on Election Day. What they can do at polling places is fairly limited.

Virginia and D.C. sue over Trump's arch, adding to legal challenges as government wants work to begin
Politics
Oct 31, 2026 2:29 PM EDT
WASHINGTON (AP) — The legal challenges to President Donald Trump's proposed memorial arch are mounting, with the District of Columbia and Virginia suing in federal court Saturday as the administration says construction could begin as early as next week.
READ MORE: 2 Trump attempts to change the D.C. landscape play out in the courts as midterms near
There are now three lawsuits calling for a halt to potential work on a monument that would rise 250 feet (76 meters) on a patch of grass off the bridge that spans the Potomac River, connecting the city with Arlington National Cemetery. That would make the arch 100 feet taller (30 meters) than the Statue of Liberty is from its base to the top of the torch.
U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan is already considering issuing an order to halt the project until the original lawsuit against the Trump administration by three Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian is resolved. She held a hearing Friday but did not immediately act, though she said she would move expeditiously.
Educate your inbox
Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics
newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else.
In the latest lawsuit, two attorneys general, Brian Schwalb of Washington and Jay Jones of Virginia, argue that "as soon as Defendants break ground on this project, they will inflict irreparable harm on both the District and Virginia. The Arch site sits at the center of a major traffic artery between the District and Virginia, in the monumental core of the capital, on an island that straddles the Potomac River. During the three-year period of construction, the Arch project will inevitably snarl traffic between the jurisdictions, produce pollution and stormwater runoff in the Potomac, interfere with emergency services, and pose numerous other challenges."
As the original plaintiffs have, they also are seeking a temporary restraining order that would slow the administration's plans to move ahead imminently with construction.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The lawsuit raises concerns about how the traffic interruption would impact emergency responses in a region where joint operations are the norm, including the January 2025 midair collision between a military helicopter and airliner that killed 67.
The Republican administration, in a recent court filing, said it had plans to seek final approval of the project, a Trump-favorite, at Thursday's meeting of the Capital National Planning Commission and possibly begin construction the same day, despite the then-two active lawsuits pending.
On Friday, the government submitted a 106-page plan for the arch that envisions a massive structure more than 12 stories high that includes a huge bronze statue of Lady Liberty with wings and carrying a torch with an eternal flame. The structure would include an observation deck with views to the east and west, an "occupied roof" and two mezzanines.
Inside the arch are rooms for program space, offices, a staff lounge, circular staircases, multiple elevators and a "fire command center." The project proposes significant traffic changes in the area, including rerouting traffic on nearby roads. Administration officials have said the arch also will have a national security function.

A third weekend of protests in France as youth-led rallies sweep Europe
World
Oct 31, 2026 1:14 PM EDT
PARIS (AP) — Hundreds of thousands of mostly young protesters took to the streets across France on Saturday in a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over living costs and education.
About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country, and Paris marches were rerouted to the capital's edge. Youth-led demonstrations were also reported in Germany and Italy.
READ MORE: France pledges new university admissions to quell student anger. But only after Macron leaves office
France's government estimated that 320,000 people protested nationwide Saturday, fewer than in previous protests but still a significant turnout. Mass protests on Oct. 17 that deteriorated into some of France's worst rioting in years drew more than 500,000 people around France, and demonstrations on Oct. 24 drew 410,000, according to government estimates. Organizers' turnout estimates are much higher.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk" of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween. Police had arrested thousands of people following riots and looting that marred the largely peaceful protest marches the previous two Saturdays.
At Porte de Bagnolet, on the eastern edge of Paris, thousands gathered behind a line of students who led the march hand in hand. Security agents from the CGT, one of France's largest labor unions, were keeping watch at the front of the gathering, while police were massed on side streets.
The Interior Ministry told reporters that of the 320,000 protesting Saturday, 70,000 people are estimated to have turned out for the main protest in Paris, which police moved outside the city center to reduce the risk of unrest around government buildings and tourist sites after a last-minute court battle.
A person releases colored smoke as protesters take part in a demonstration organized by labor unions as part of nationwide protests called by the "Yellow Vests" movement joined by French high school and university students against the cost of living and rising fuel prices, in Paris on Oct. 31, 2026. Photo by Abdul Saboor/Reuters
The marchers' grievances are diverse.
Each group carried its own banner: high school students, climate activists and people angry about the cost of living.
A few Halloween costumes stood out in the crowd, including a zombie Michael Jackson from "Thriller," a pirate and a Spider-Man. Protesters waited calmly, chanting and singing through megaphones.
Corentin Cabreux, a 21-year-old student, said that he lives in a state-run student residence where "there are damp stains all along the bottom of my walls, whole sections peeling off, cockroaches everywhere, rats."
He said that he hoped Saturday's protest would be festive in honor of Halloween, to counter the image of violence that has attached itself to France's protests.
Police impose curfew and other measures
The rallies started last month as a movement of high school students protesting neglected buildings, teacher shortages and a university admissions system seen as unfair to disadvantaged students. Labor unions and others angry at President Emmanuel Macron joined in with a variety of demands.
While the vast majority of protesters have been peaceful, groups of troublemakers routinely target police with fireworks and projectiles. Some protests have degenerated into rioting and looting — including unrest on Oct. 17 that appeared to take the government by surprise. Police have responded with tear gas, dispersion grenades, water cannons and other tactics that have resulted in severe injuries.
WATCH: Why French students are leading massive protests across the country
Macron said that Saturday's marches would stay out of city centers to protect shops. Police also barred people from entering Place de la Republique and Les Halles from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. Saturday and Sunday.
Unaccompanied minors face a separate 9 p.m. curfew around the Champs-Elysees. A Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement.
Protests are also taking place in Germany, Italy and Spain
In Germany, a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" — roughly "Gen Z's got this" — rallied in many cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life," and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that more than 180,000 people had signed up online, but as of Saturday afternoon only several thousand marched in various cities across the country.
Young protesters also gathered at Berlin's Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing.
"We call for more money to be invested in social services and education, as well as in climate protection — in short, in our future — because we are the ones who will be affected by this the longest and who will have to live with it," high school student Lara Breitenbach said.
Janelle Schulz, another high school student from Berlin, also said that the authorities had to invest more money in education.
"At my school, the ceiling is collapsing because of water damage, nothing is being done about it, we have a shortage of teachers, the toilets are broken," she said.

When will we know 2026 midterm election results? It may take some time, but that's normal
Politics
Oct 31, 2026 1:02 PM EDT
This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.
If you go to bed on election night and don't know who won a midterm congressional race, that's normal. And if you wake up the next morning and find that a candidate who was behind hours earlier has since pulled ahead, that's normal, too.
That won't stop some politicians and their allies from spreading misinformation during vote counting.
WATCH: How does The Associated Press call 2026 midterm election winners? 4 things to know
In past elections, elected leaders, candidates and social media users have spread falsehoods that "late night" arrivals of "ballot dumps" or "suitcases" of ballots are signs of fraud, or that only Democratic-led cities take days to count votes.
Some states such as Florida often complete the majority of their unofficial counts in fewer hours or days than elsewhere. But it is not a sign of fraud if other places need more time.
"States are neither fast or slow, they all count and certify the results in accordance with the laws passed by their state legislature," said Ryan Macias, an election technology and cybersecurity expert. "What is fast or slow is how quickly the media can collect sufficient evidence to confidently predict the winner, which is typically based on the margin of victory."
Educate your inbox
Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics
newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else.
Voters can help elections run smoothly. People who vote by mail, for instance, should not wait until the last minute to submit their ballots. Many election offices provide secure drop boxes to speed the return of mailed ballots. The U.S. Postal Service recommends that voters mail in their ballot at least one week before the deadline.
"There are always a handful of really close Senate and House races in which the winner will not be determined for several days or, in the cases of Alaska and California, as much as a week or two," said Joe Lenski, executive vice president of SSRS, which conducts a national exit poll on Election Day.
Control of the U.S. Senate could come down to a handful of close races with large numbers of ballots to count.
No state is required to complete the official count on election night. State laws set deadlines to certify final results, often weeks later.
Here's a look at what could influence the timing of unofficial results.
Close margins
Polls and nonpartisan analysis show many U.S. Senate races are competitive, including in Michigan, Maine, Iowa, Alaska, Kansas and Texas. If the counts are close in the first few hours or even days after polls close, media outlets may have to wait for officials to count more ballots until journalists can project a winner. Some close races could end in a recount completed days or weeks later. In 2018, three Florida statewide races were settled in recounts.
Candidates who lead early in the vote count may not ultimately win. In 2020, Donald Trump was up by more than 100,000 votes in Wisconsin early in the night, but the picture quickly shifted after Milwaukee's central count finished processing mail-in votes around 3:30 a.m local time. The late boost for Joe Biden from Milwaukee was expected, especially because Wisconsin's mail-in ballots tend to skew Democratic.
The pattern of when votes are counted — and what political leanings those jurisdictions' voters tend to have — varies by state.
Mail ballot volume and receipt deadlines
It takes time to process mail ballots. Election workers must verify voter identity, for example, by matching envelope signatures against registration records.
Most states, including Florida, require that mail ballots be received by Election Day. But some states allow voters to return ballots later as long as they were postmarked by Election Day.
In California, which runs nearly all-mail elections, ballots postmarked by Election Day and received up to a week later are permitted. The U.S. Supreme Court in June upheld the right of states to have such a policy, a blow to Trump, who says he wants a faster process and has spread falsehoods about California's vote counting.
READ MORE: 5 expert takeaways on 2026 midterm election security
Ohio passed a law in 2025 that said most absentee ballots must be received by the close of polls on Election Day; previously it had a four-day grace period.
In California, counties must count and report the results from most ballots by the 13th day after the election. There are some exceptions to that, including for provisional ballots and mail ballots with signature verification needs; election officials should be done counting those within 30 days after the election.
In U.S. House races, there are always a handful of districts that are not called on election night or the day after, mostly in California, Lenski said.
Last minute absentee ballot submissions: A Michigan case study
When thousands of voters procrastinate sending in their mail ballots until the last minute, it takes election workers extra time to process and count those ballots. In past elections, some people have spread falsehoods about such "delays" in places like Detroit, pointing to vans with ballots arriving late at night as evidence of foul play.

Congo's Ebola deaths top 5,000 as fear of continent-wide spread mounts
World
Oct 31, 2026 11:25 AM EDT
BUNIA, Congo (AP) — Deaths in Congo's Ebola outbreak have topped 5,000 as the country grapples with the relentless spread of the disease and cases are recorded in other African countries, the latest government data on Saturday shows.
Data from the Congolese Ministry of Health showed that the disease has killed 5,026 people out of 10,351 infected, at a nearly 50% lethality rate. The surge is sparking concerns among experts regarding the authorities' ability to contain the deadly virus.
The latest outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, was declared in mid-May, catching authorities by surprise. They have since struggled to manage it.
READ MORE: 1st confirmed Ebola patient in Nigeria evacuated to Switzerland
It is already the second deadliest Ebola outbreak in history, second only to a two-year-long West Africa outbreak between 2014 and 2016, which killed 11,000 people across multiple countries.
"It is a very tragic milestone because it is just not a number," said Dr. Patrick Otim, a programme area manager with the World Health Organization. "It is families and communities that have been devastated by this outbreak. The number also shows the severity of this outbreak."
2,788 people have recovered from the virus so far. The Bundibugyo virus has no known vaccine or treatment, but health workers treat patients based on symptoms.
One-third of people who have died did not get to receive any care
Since May, the disease has spread to 67 out of the country's 178 health zones in eight of 26 provinces. Fifty of the affected 67 health zones have active cases.
The virus has been concentrated in the eastern region of Congo, especially in Ituri and North Kivu, which have emerged as the epicenters with 9,782 total confirmed cases and 4,792 total deaths.
Authorities are still struggling with tracing contacts and testing, key components in the race to curb the outbreak.
READ MORE: Nigeria confirms Ebola case in its capital as woman who arrived from Uganda tests positive
According to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about 80% of new cases are coming from outside the chain of monitored contacts, meaning an overwhelming share of infections are coming from unknown chains of transmission to health authorities.
Also, one-third of recorded deaths are victims who have died outside of treatment centers, before being tested for Ebola, WHO's Otim said. These issues, health officials say, contribute to community transmission outside of the immediate purview of health workers who can effectively manage infection in accordance with medical protocols.
"These are people we never had opportunity to try to save them and it is one of the biggest concerns for us in this outbreak. How do we try to reach people early to get them to come to health facilities to get a fighting chance to survive?" Otim said.
'The outbreak is stretching everyone responding to it'
The explosive number of infections in Congo comes on the heels of a long list of issues that have hamstrung efforts to contain the outbreak.
The eastern region of Congo, where the outbreak is concentrated, plays host to a conflict between the government and an array of armed groups, most prominently the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group, and there is also an Islamist insurgency in the border areas with Uganda, where the Allied Democratic Forces carry out attacks, limiting the reach of healthcare workers.
Also, there is widespread disbelief among the population, which has led to a series of attacks on health workers and health facilities. A nurse was killed while responding to an Ebola alert last week, and a politician from the ruling party was killed in September after advocating for health measures on the radio.
Health workers have gone on multiple strikes, shutting down facilities where they treat infected people, citing long delays in payments by the government.
On Friday, workers at an Ebola treatment center in Tchomia, in Ituri, downed tools, demanding four months of unpaid wages. At the center, there are currently five confirmed Ebola patients and 10 suspected cases under care.
READ MORE: Congo's confirmed Ebola cases surpass 9,000 as containment efforts falter
"We are tired of requesting our salaries. If they want to pay us, they will. ... Today, being able to feed our families has become a real problem," Moise Mugenyi, one of the striking workers, told the AP.
Dr. Justin Mukonkole, acting head of response operations in Ituri, said the workers should be patient while the government responds to their demands.
Similar situations have played out in other health zones like Beni in North Kivu, where services in some treatment centers have ground to a halt. Alain Siwako, an elected public official in Beni, said cases are spiralling in Beni because of a lack of fuel and financial resources from the central government.
"Across Ituri and North Kivu, this outbreak is stretching everyone responding to it, including the communities themselves," Rose Tchwenko, Country Director for the DRC, Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps), said.

What to know about the $6.3B hack on Binance, likely the biggest-ever crypto theft
World
Oct 31, 2026 11:14 AM EDT
Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said Friday that hackers stole more than $6 billion in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record. Blockchain firms have pointed to the attack coming from a North Korean hacking unit.
The company said it has reserved more than $6.34 billion of company funds to cover the stolen assets and was beginning to recover assets for users. Binance worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets.
WATCH: $6 billion cryptocurrency heist puts investors on edge
The cryptocurrency exchange has promised to cover all losses, and it has been sharing regular updates on its social media channels as it uncovers more information about the hack.
"We are working nonstop to resolve this," Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said Friday in a video posted to X.
In an exchange Friday with reporters at the White House, President Donald Trump said U.S. officials were investigating the Binance hack. Asked whether North Korea was involved, Trump said: "We're looking at that."
Here's what we know about the hack, possible North Korean involvement and Binance's investigation.
North Korean hackers are suspected in the attack
Binance said on X that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, but that a subsequent investigation uncovered additional "points of breach."
U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm TRM, in a post on its website late Thursday, attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit. "We make this judgment with high confidence," the firm said.
"An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," TRM said. "Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists."
Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, its co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin wrote on X.
Asked about the potential ties to North Korea, a Binance spokesperson said only that the company is "working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice."
Experts have said that North Korea turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities in recent years as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.
In December 2022, South Korea's spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets over the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea's capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the world's best.
Many are calling this the biggest crypto theft on record
While about half of the stolen assets were frozen, there is evidence that the hackers already are transferring and converting some of what wasn't recovered, said Garrick Hileman, an independent cryptocurrency analyst.
"Like in money laundering, you bring in the stolen goods and launder those through a mixer or tumbler," he said. "You mix it in with other cryptos, and it's harder to track."
How long it will take the hackers to turn that into something usable isn't clear, he said. "The bottom line is there are places in the world where you can take your bitcoin and get that converted," Hileman said.
READ MORE: Binance flags 'potential security issue,' says approximately $6.3 billion impacted
TRM and several other crypto firms and experts have said the hack represents the largest cryptocurrency theft on record.
In February of last year, another cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, suffered a $1.5 billion hit when it was hacked. The FBI said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the hack. TRM listed the Bybit hack when it referenced similarities between the Binance hack and previous attacks linked to TraderTraitor.
Binance's founder, Changpeng Zhao, wrote on X that while Binance's hack might be the largest in terms of its dollar value, previous attacks on other companies like the crypto exchange Mt. Gox have had a more substantial impact in terms of the bitcoin amount affected, he said.
Experts warn this scale of hacking could become more commonplace.
"A cyber attack of this level is a matter of when, not if, particularly alongside the rise of AI," said Andy Ward, a senior vice president at Absolute Security. "Cyber threats are becoming more sophisticated and widespread as ever, and it is likely only a matter of time before an even larger hack, with even greater financial fallout, makes headlines."
Where experts — and Binance — say things went wrong
The hack has raised questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, co-founder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab.
"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and that are conne

G20 foreign ministers end Atlanta meeting without consensus on key issues
Politics
Updated on Oct 31, 2026 2:12 PM EDT — Published on
Oct 31, 2026 11:00 AM EDT
ATLANTA (AP) — Top diplomats from the Group of 20 largest world economies wrapped up two days of talks Saturday without reaching consensus on several critical global security issues after divisions, notably over Russia's war with Ukraine, overshadowed the start of the Atlanta meeting.
As a result, the group did not release a joint communique but will rather rely on a chairman's statement summarizing the talks, which Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he would release later Saturday.
WATCH: Rubio welcomes G20 foreign ministers to Atlanta at 'critical moment'
"I wouldn't pretend to you today that we are close to finding universally accepted solutions to these problems," Rubio told reporters at a news conference marking the end of the meetings.
"But," he said, "I do think that among the G-20 represented here are countries that are working together to solve some of them, particularly in the realm of supply chains and critical minerals."
Rubio had said the first day of the session was "very productive" and hosted sideline talks with his counterparts from Australia, India and Japan on Saturday before leading the final G20 event. That discussion on supply chains examined freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red, Black and South China seas.
Educate your inbox
Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics
newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else.
"I made clear to our partners that secure supply chains are essential for growth," Rubio said in a social media post on X. "Critical trade routes including the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb Strait must remain secure and open to commerce. And we must continue to strengthen and expand critical mineral supply chains to protect our future."
At a reception for G20 participants Friday night, Rubio sounded optimistic. "Together, I think that we are mapping a vibrant, dynamic, and bold economic future, one that will pioneer new horizons for the entire world," he said.
The traditional group photo was canceled
Rubio had opened the talks Friday with an appeal for unity, but then canceled the traditional group photo of the foreign ministers. European diplomats objected to the inclusion of Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and threatened to boycott or walk out of the snapshot.
Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski, who was representing his country for the first time as a guest at a G20 meeting, said he was not surprised by the failure to reach consensus.
"We have wars going on, and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it's very difficult to agree on a common line," he told reporters.
Other participants in the meetings, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the private talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month's summit of G20 leaders hosted by President Donald Trump in Florida a success.
These diplomats said a chairman's statement had long been the plan because of the deep differences among the attendees, including over the Russia-Ukraine war, the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, U.S. tariffs and Chinese moves in the South China Sea. All have contributed to spikes in the global cost of fuel as well as uncertainty about trade.
They described the opening session as cordial but said Russia's position on Ukraine was unyielding — as was its opposition to Poland's membership in the G20. They said the disagreements also included the Trump administration's decision not to invite G20 member South Africa over the objections of others.
Russia's presence at G20 gathering roils Europeans
Before the meeting began, some G20 countries had expressed concern that the U.S. invited Russia during its heightened attacks on Ukraine, especially after Trump pushed ties with Ukraine to new lows by waiving fresh sanctions on Moscow and temporarily limiting logistical and intelligence assistance.
The State Department, however, announced Friday that it had approved a proposed $2.1 billion sale of Patriot air defense interceptors for Ukraine.
READ MORE: Rubio says U.S. pressure on NATO allies to boost defense spending is 'not hostile'
Lavrov said Moscow would not allow a situation in which Ukraine poses a "military threat to legitimate security interests of the Russian Federation."
Lavrov has traveled only infrequently to NATO member states since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and resulting severe sanctions were imposed on Moscow. It is unclear whether Russian President Vladimir Putin will accept Trump's invitation to attend the summit at Trump's Miami golf club in December.
The Iran war hangs over the G20 event
Also hanging over the G20 meeting was the prospect of new U.S. military intervention in Iran. That has put the region, including G20 member Saudi Arabia, on edge. Rubio met on Friday with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan, as well as Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, whose country has been a key mediator.
The Associated Press has reported that U.S. officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military strikes against Iran after U.S. elections

Evacuees fleeing Oleshky reunite with family at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border
World
Updated on Oct 31, 2026 2:19 PM EDT — Published on
Oct 31, 2026 10:47 AM EDT
CHERNIHIV REGION, Ukraine (AP) — Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky crossed into Ukrainian-held territory Saturday in a major rescue operation carried out under the most significant truce since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine 4½ years ago.
Evacuees wrapped in blue and yellow Ukrainian flags stepped off buses at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border and reunited with family members. Volunteers with hand-drawn welcome signs handed out coffee to the weary travelers who had traveled by bus and plane through Russia and Belarus. Residents of nearby villages lined the highway waving flags and flashlights to greet the convoy.
READ MORE: Aid operation and evacuations in Oleshky amid brief truce agreed to by Russia and Ukraine
Tetiana Leonidivna, 71, thanked the Ukrainian soldiers who helped her to flee.
"We love them, we love them," she said through tears. "We know that they are protecting us. And a deep bow to them, and a deep bow to their parents, for having such children. I am proud, I am simply proud."
The ceasefire in Ukraine's southern Kherson region began early Tuesday and was expected to continue through Sunday evening. The White House has said U.S. first lady Melania Trump helped to broker the localized deal, while Pope Leo XIV pressed Russia and Ukraine to allow aid deliveries and evacuations.
Evacuees and their families express fear and hope
Relatives and volunteers with the Red Cross, Doctors Without Borders and World Central Kitchen welcomed the evacuees as they arrived at the border, ready to provide aid and food, including for their pets.
Holding a cigarette between shaking fingers, 48-year-old Ivan Yevhenovych described his last months in Oleshky.
"It was very difficult. There were a lot of drones. It was hard to move around the streets," he said. "Since spring, there hasn't really been any staple food left. People had a little bit of their own reserves. We are thrifty people."
He said landmines or drone strikes were killing residents every day.
WATCH: Inside a Ukrainian city hit by Russian drones during the Starlink disruption
An estimated 2,000 people remained in Oleshky when the temporary truce took hold. They were offered the choice of being evacuated to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.
"Many people stayed behind and didn't want to leave," Yevhenovych said. "Some for their houses, some for their animals."
Ukrainian authorities, seeking to protect those who remained and safeguard future humanitarian missions, have not said how many residents evacuated Oleshky and have restricted details of their route. Melania Trump posted on social media Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.
Liza Paliy, 19, waited at the border for her father, whom she last saw more than 2½ years earlier when she fled the occupied city with her mother and sister.
"We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately, two years have already passed," she said.
Ukraine and Russia call the operation a success
Ukrainian police officers with emergency services and Red Cross employees handle pet animals of residents evacuated during a humanitarian mission from the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, returning to Ukrainian-controlled territory, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, at an undisclosed location on Oct. 31, 2026. Photo by Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, hailed the humanitarian mission a win.
"This is an extremely important moment. Behind us are difficult negotiations, agreements, preparations, and an enormous amount of work. But most importantly, the people who waited so long to be rescued are finally safe," he said in an online post.
Lubinets said evacuees ranged in age from just over a year old to 94, and they brought pets, including dogs, cats, a parrot and a raccoon. He said he hoped the Oleshky truce can be replicated elsewhere, saying it "could form the basis of a new mechanism for responding to the most difficult humanitarian crises."
Yana Lantratova, Russia's human rights commissioner, said both sides have agreed to conduct regular humanitarian missions in and around Oleshky. Lubinets did not mention this development.
"The mission has concluded, but, unfortunately, living conditions in Oleshky remain extremely difficult," she said. "We will make every effort to support those residents who have made the decision to stay."
Some Oleshky evacuees who chose to move to Russian-occupied territory were taken to a temporary shelter in Simferopol, Lantratova said. The city is in Ukraine's Crimean Peninsula, which Moscow annexed in 2014.
"After everything they have endured and a long journey, it is essential for these people to rest, recover, and feel cared for. However, support should not be limited to just a roof over their heads and a hot meal," she said in a social media post.
The U.S. approves Patriot missile sale for Ukraine
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday welcomed U.S. approval of Ukraine's purchase of 500 PAC-3 Patriot interceptors but urged partners to also supply weapons
